interviewQuestions.question: How would you design driver-rider matching to handle constant location updates efficiently?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate two very different workloads on the same data: a high-frequency write path (every available driver pings its location every few seconds) and a lower-frequency but latency-sensitive read path (a rider's match request needs the nearest available driver right now). Scanning all drivers on every match request looks fine at small scale and falls over as the fleet grows.

So I'd back both paths with a spatial index — a geohash grid or quadtree — where a location ping is a cheap, localized update to one cell, and a match query only touches nearby cells instead of the whole driver set.

I'd close by noting the actual claim of a driver still needs an atomic conditional write, since the index only helps you find candidates — it doesn't prevent two riders from racing for the same one.

**Testing:** whether you can separate read and write cost concerns on the same data structure, rather than treating "add an index" as the whole answer.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Efficient driver-rider matching

interviewQuestions.question: How would you extend this design to support pooled rides or scheduled-in-advance trips?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
For pooling, I'd start from the fact that a single `Trip` no longer maps to one rider — I'd introduce a `TripLeg` or similar concept so one driver's trip can carry multiple riders with different pickup/drop points, and the matching problem becomes "which pending requests share a reasonable route with an in-progress trip," not just nearest-driver.

For scheduled trips, the request doesn't need a driver assigned immediately — it needs to be held and matched shortly before the scheduled time, when driver availability is actually known. I'd model this as a separate `ScheduledRequest` that a background process promotes into a normal match flow at the right time, rather than bending the real-time matching path to also handle far-future requests.

In both cases I'd flag that the core entities (Trip, Driver, matching) stay largely intact — it's the request and assignment logic in front of them that changes.

**Testing:** whether you can extend a design without a full rewrite, by isolating what's actually new.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Extending to pooling and scheduled trips

interviewQuestions.question: Why does a trip need its own explicit lifecycle of states rather than a single boolean like 'active'?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from what a boolean can't distinguish: REQUESTED (no driver yet), MATCHED (driver assigned, en route to pickup), IN_PROGRESS (rider onboard), and COMPLETED all look identical to a flag that's just "true." But the valid operations differ sharply at each point — a rider can cancel for free while REQUESTED, cancellation after MATCHED may incur a fee since a driver already committed, and cancellation is impossible once IN_PROGRESS.

So I'd model `Trip` with an explicit status field and a transition table, the same discipline I'd apply to any stateful entity: each transition names its preconditions (matching only succeeds from REQUESTED, starting only from MATCHED) and its side effects (matching notifies the driver, completing triggers fare calculation). A single boolean would push all of that branching logic into whichever code path happens to touch the trip next, scattering rules that belong in one place.

Concretely, this also protects against bugs like completing a trip that was never actually started, or matching a driver to a trip that a rider already cancelled — both become illegal transitions the state machine simply rejects, rather than bugs discovered in production.

**Testing:** whether you reach for an explicit state machine as the default for any entity with meaningfully different valid operations per stage, not just when a slide happens to call it out.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why an explicit trip lifecycle

interviewQuestions.question: Why use a Strategy for fare calculation instead of a single method with conditionals for surge, city, and ride-type pricing?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd name the failure mode a conditional-heavy `calculateFare()` produces first: every new pricing rule (a new city's tax rules, a new ride tier, a promo) adds another branch to one already-large method, and testing one rule in isolation means tracing through all the others to make sure they didn't interact.

With a `FareStrategy` interface, each pricing rule — `SurgeFareStrategy`, `CityBaseFareStrategy`, `PromoDiscountStrategy` — is its own class implementing one `calculate(trip)` method, and `Trip` or a `FareCalculator` just holds a reference to whichever strategy applies, or composes several. Adding a new city's fare rule means writing one new class and registering it, never touching the classes that already work and are already tested.

The concrete payoff shows up at review time: a bug report about surge pricing in one city sends you straight to one class, not a 200-line method where every early-return could be the culprit. I'd also flag the cost of this: it's more files and more indirection for a genuinely simple case, so I wouldn't reach for Strategy if there were only ever one pricing rule with no foreseeable variation.

**Testing:** whether you can justify a pattern by its concrete payoff (isolated testing, safe extension) rather than reciting 'it's more flexible' as a slogan.
